title: Estimation of national, regional, and global prevalence of alcohol use during pregnancy and fetal alcohol syndrome: A systematic review and meta-analysis

claims.statement: In eight unrelated children (five girls and three boys; three Native American, three Black and two White; aged 3 to 57 months when their development was tested) evaluated at a dysmorphology unit in Seattle and born to mothers who met the 1972 National Council on Alcoholism criteria for alcoholism (for more than 2 to 23 years, mean 9.4; delirium tremens in 5 of the 6 with a record, two of them in hospital with it during the pregnancy) and who drank heavily throughout pregnancy (no amounts recorded; none known to be dependent on another drug), a report that its authors call apparently the first to link a mother's alcoholism with abnormal development of the child's body (Jones et al., 1973; funded by US federal maternal and child health and National Institutes of Health grants and the National Foundation–March of Dimes; no conflict statement) describes a shared pattern: growth deficiency starting before birth in all eight (mean birth length and weight at the 50th percentile for 33 and 34 weeks of gestation, against a mean of 38 weeks; birth weights 1,550 to 2,500 g) with no catch-up later, even with adequate food during hospital stays for six of them or in foster care for three (after age 1, growth in length 65% and weight gain 38% of normal); short palpebral fissures (eye openings) in all eight; developmental delay in all eight (IQ or developmental index 57 to 83 in six and below 50 in one; none in the normal range, as the authors judged it); a small head in seven; an underdeveloped upper jaw in seven; altered palm creases in six; joint anomalies in five; heart anomalies in five (three of them murmurs that went away, taken to be septal defects that had closed); and folds of skin at the inner corner of the eye in four. The paper does not use the name fetal alcohol syndrome and refers to the pattern only as a syndrome; the two prevalence reviews read for this page date the first description of FAS to November 1973, one of them citing a later 1973 paper by two of the same authors with the name in its title, which was not read. This is a description of eight selected children, not a measure of how often the pattern follows heavy drinking in pregnancy or of what causes it: four children were recognised first and two more were found because they had the same features, possibly milder cases were left out on purpose, there was no comparison group and no count of children of mothers with alcoholism who were unaffected, the examiners knew the mothers' histories, the amount and timing of drinking were not recorded, smoking and other drug use were not reported, nutrition was only partly recorded, and poverty could not be separated out (all the families were on welfare); the authors nonetheless concluded that their data establish that maternal alcoholism can cause serious abnormal development before birth. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
claims.magnitude: Jones et al. 1973 (descriptive counts; no comparison group, no statistical tests). Table II, features present out of 8: developmental delay 8, microcephaly 7, prenatal growth deficiency 8, postnatal growth deficiency 8, short palpebral fissures 8, maxillary hypoplasia with relative prognathism 7, epicanthal folds 4, joint anomalies 5, altered palmar crease pattern 6, cardiac anomaly 5 (three presumed ventricular septal defects that closed). Table I: maternal alcoholism 7, 3, 4, 11, 2+, 10, 23 and 15 years (mean 9.4); delirium tremens 5 of 6 with data; maternal age at the birth 22 to 40 (mean 31.7); gestational age 34 to 44 weeks (mean 38); birth weight 1,550 to 2,500 g (mean 2,034); birth length 38 to 47 cm (mean 43.6); breech presentation 3 of 8. Growth: mean birth length and weight at the 50th percentile for 33 and 34 weeks of gestation; after 1 year of age, linear growth 65% and weight gain 38% of normal; mean daily weight gain 9 g against 26.6 g in upper-middle-class Seattle children and 24.4 g in high-risk children in a local programme; head circumference below the 3rd percentile at birth in 7 of 8 and at 1 year in 5 of 6 with data. Table III (age at testing 3 to 57 months): IQ or mental development index 59, 83, 75, 57, 79, 70 and below 50 (one child not scored); fine motor dysfunction in 5 of 6 tested; repetitive self-stimulating behaviour in 5.

claims.statement: In children and youth in the general population (special populations, such as children in care, left out of the estimates), fetal alcohol spectrum disorder (FASD), the umbrella term for the effects of alcohol before birth, which includes fetal alcohol syndrome (FAS), partial FAS and alcohol-related neurodevelopmental disorder, was estimated in one systematic review with meta-analysis and modelling (Lange et al., 2017; 24 studies, 1,416 children and youth with FASD aged 0 to 16, from 8 countries; no funding statement; no conflicts declared) at 7.7 per 1,000 worldwide (95% CI 4.9 to 11.7), about 8 in 1,000, and FAS alone, in a companion review by the same team (Popova et al., 2017; 62 studies from 19 countries; funded by the authors' institute; no competing interests declared), at 14.6 per 10,000 people (9.4 to 23.3), about 1.5 in 1,000 (editors' conversion). By WHO region, FASD per 1,000 and FAS per 10,000 were 7.8 and 14.8 in the African region, 8.8 and 16.6 in the Americas, 0.1 and 0.2 in the Eastern Mediterranean, 19.8 and 37.4 in the European region, 1.4 and 2.7 in South-East Asia, and 6.7 and 12.7 in the Western Pacific. These world and regional figures are mostly calculated, not counted: FASD was pooled from studies for 6 countries and FAS for 7, and for every other country (181 and 180 of 187) the reviews divided the estimated share of women who drank during pregnancy, itself mostly predicted (see the answer on drinking in pregnancy), by a fixed ratio from a few countries, 13 women who drank per child with FASD and 67 per child with FAS, so the world figures are close to the world drinking figure of 9.8% divided by 13 and by 67 (editors' arithmetic). These ratios are averages across countries, not the chance for any one pregnancy, and neither review could examine the amount, pattern or timing of drinking. In the 24 FASD studies, figures ranged from 0.1 per 1,000 in a national Australian study and 0.4 to 5.6 per 1,000 in three French clinic studies of newborns to 63.9 to 207.5 per 1,000 in six studies of school-age children in South Africa's Northern and Western Cape in which researchers sought out and examined children; pooled national estimates were 53.3 per 1,000 for Croatia, 45.0 for Italy and 111.1 for South Africa. In eight select studies of special populations (adopted children or children in care, a correctional population, Indigenous populations, a low-income rural population, people in psychiatric care), FASD figures ran from 40.0 to 521.1 per 1,000. The authors say the diagnostic systems used differ and lack reliability, that studies were often done where many cases were expected, and that self-reported drinking may be undercounted. The two reviews' ratios imply about 5 children with FASD for each child with FAS (67 / 13, editors' arithmetic), while the FAS review cites a ratio of about 9 or 10. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
claims.magnitude: Lange et al. 2017 (FASD per 1,000 children and youth, Table 2; 95% CI by Monte Carlo simulation): worldwide 7.7 (4.9–11.7); WHO African region 7.8 (5.4–10.7); Americas 8.8 (6.4–13.2); Eastern Mediterranean 0.1 (0.1–0.5); European 19.8 (14.1–28.0); South-East Asia 1.4 (0.6–5.3); Western Pacific 6.7 (4.5–11.7). Five highest countries, in alphabetical order: Belarus 36.6 (23.7–53.2; predicted), Croatia 53.3 (30.9–81.2; meta-analysis), Ireland 47.5 (28.0–73.6; predicted), Italy 45.0 (35.1–56.1; meta-analysis), South Africa 111.1 (71.1–158.4; meta-analysis); 76 of 187 countries above 10 per 1,000 (1%), almost all by prediction. Study level (Table 1, per 1,000): Australia 0.1 (national; 92 cases in 1,533,333) and 1.7; Canada 5.3; Croatia 40.8 and 66.8; France 0.4, 5.4 and 5.6 in newborns and 66.0 on Réunion Island (75 cases in 1,320, which is 56.8, editors' arithmetic); Italy 40.5 and 47.1; Norway 1.1; South Africa 63.9 to 207.5; USA 5.1 to 33.5. Ratio: 1 FASD case per 13 women who drank in pregnancy, which the authors turn into about 630,000 children born with FASD each year. Special populations (Figure 2 legend, per 1,000): 40.0 to 521.1 in eight select studies, 5.2 to 67.7 times the global estimate. Popova et al. 2017 (FAS per 10,000 people, Table): worldwide 14.6 (9.4–23.3); African 14.8 (8.9–21.5); Americas 16.6 (11.0–24.0); Eastern Mediterranean 0.2 (0.2–0.9); European 37.4 (24.7–54.2); South-East Asia 2.7 (1.3–8.1); Western Pacific 12.7 (7.7–19.4). Five highest countries, in alphabetical order: Belarus 69.1 (42.1–103.5; predicted), Croatia 115.2 (34.8–236.0), Ireland 89.7 (50.4–142.8; predicted), Italy 82.1 (42.1–134.6), South Africa 585.3 (430.7–761.7). Ratio: 1 FAS case per 67 women who drank in pregnancy (from Australia, Canada, Croatia, France, Italy, South Korea and the USA), which the authors turn into about 119,000 children born with FAS each year by applying the prevalence per 10,000 people to 81,536,534 live births. The FAS review cites an earlier estimate (Abel, 1995; not read) of 4.3% FAS among children born to women who drank heavily in pregnancy (on average two or more drinks a day, or five to six at a time; no drink size in grams). Editors' arithmetic: 14.6 per 10,000 is 1.5 per 1,000; 9.8% / 13 = 7.5 per 1,000 and 9.8% / 67 = 14.6 per 10,000; 67 / 13 = 5.2 FASD cases per FAS case.

claims.statement: In women in the general population who were pregnant or had recently given birth, any alcohol use during pregnancy, as reported in studies published from 1984 to mid-2014 (328 studies with data from 50 countries; studies of special populations, such as Indigenous women, adolescents and women with an alcohol use disorder, left out, although the review notes that drinking in pregnancy can be much higher in some such groups), was estimated in one systematic review with meta-analysis and modelling (Popova et al., 2017; funded by the authors' institute, with no external funding sought; no competing interests declared) at 9.8% worldwide (95% CI 8.9% to 11.1%), about 10 in 100 pregnant women, in estimates labelled 2012 and weighted by live births. By WHO region it was 10.0% (8.5% to 11.8%) in the African region, 11.2% (9.4% to 12.6%) in the Americas, 0.2% (0.1% to 0.9%) in the Eastern Mediterranean, 25.2% (21.6% to 29.6%) in the European region, about 25 in 100, 1.8% (0.9% to 5.1%) in South-East Asia and 8.6% (4.5% to 11.6%) in the Western Pacific; country estimates ran from 0% (five countries, all by prediction) to 60.4% (42.8% to 76.8%), and the five highest were all in the European region. Most of these figures are model estimates, not measurements: studies were pooled for 29 countries, and the other 158, including 21 of the 50 countries with data (editors' arithmetic), were given a value predicted from national income, women's average alcohol consumption and WHO region. The data are self-reports, which the authors say may undercount drinking; the amount and frequency of drinking, and so binge drinking, were not analysed because the studies reported them inconsistently or not at all, timing in pregnancy was not analysed either, and no drink size is defined; and studies published over three decades are pooled into one set of figures labelled 2012 (editors' observation). Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
claims.magnitude: Popova et al. 2017, Table (any alcohol use during pregnancy in the general population, 2012, weighted by live births; 95% CI by Monte Carlo simulation): worldwide 9.8% (8.9–11.1); WHO African region 10.0% (8.5–11.8); Americas 11.2% (9.4–12.6); Eastern Mediterranean 0.2% (0.1–0.9); European 25.2% (21.6–29.6); South-East Asia 1.8% (0.9–5.1); Western Pacific 8.6% (4.5–11.6). The five highest countries, in alphabetical order: Belarus 46.6% (42.4–50.7; predicted), Denmark 45.8% (30.9–61.2), Ireland 60.4% (42.8–76.8), Russia 36.5% (18.7–56.4), UK 41.3% (lower limit 32.9; upper limit misprinted); 0% (predicted) in Kuwait, Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates. Pooled by random-effects meta-analysis for 29 countries; predicted by fractional response regression for 158. As counts: about 10 in 100 pregnant women worldwide and about 25 in 100 in the European region (editors' rounding).
